Cosmology, Black Holes

and

Shock Waves Beyond the Hubble Length

December 18, 2002

J​o​e​l​S​m​o​l​l​e​rB​l​a​k​e​T​e​m​p​l​e\begin{array}[]{ccc}Joel\ Smoller&Blake\ Temple\end{array}
Abstract

We construct exact, entropy satisfying shock wave solutions of the Einstein equations for a perfect fluid which extend the Oppeheimer-Snyder (OS) model to the case of non-zero pressure, inside the Black Hole. These solutions put forth a new Cosmological Model in which the expanding Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) universe emerges from the Big Bang with a shock wave at the leading edge of the expansion, analogous to a classical shock wave explosion. This explosion is large enough to account for the enormous scale on which the galaxies and the background radiation appear uniform. In these models, the shock wave must lie beyond one Hubble length from the FRW center, this threshhold being the boundary across which the bounded mass lies inside its own Schwarzshild radius, 2​M/r>1,2M/r>1, and thus the shock wave solution evolves inside a Black Hole. The entropy condition, which breaks the time symmetry, implies that the shock wave must weaken until it eventually settles down to a zero pressure OS interface, bounding a finite total mass, that emerges from the White Hole event horizon of an ambient Schwarzschild spacetime. However, unlike shock matching outside a Black Hole, the equation of state p=c23​ρ,p=\frac{c^{2}}{3}\rho, the equation of state at the earliest stage of Big Bang physics, is distinguished at the instant of the Big Bang—for this equation of state alone, the shock wave emerges from the Big Bang at a finite nonzero speed, the speed of light, decelerating to a subluminous wave from that time onward. These shock wave solutions indicate a new cosmological model in which the Big Bang arises from a localized explosion occurring inside the Black Hole of an asymptotically flat Schwarzschild spacetime.

1 Introduction

In the standard model of cosmology based on a critically expanding, (k=0k=0), Friedmann-Robertson-Walker (FRW) metric, the universe is infinite at each instant after the Big Bang, [11, 21, 24]. The Hubble constant, which measures the recessional velocity of the galaxies, applies to the entire flat space 𝐑3{\bf R}^{3}—that is, it applies to an entire universe of infinite mass and extent—at each fixed positive time in the standard model. In this paper we present a new cosmological model in which the expansion of the galaxies is a bounded expansion of finite total mass, and the Hubble law applies only to a bounded region of spacetime, (c.f. [21]). If the observed expansion of the galaxies actually only applies to a localized region of spacetime, then it follows that there must be a wave at the leading edge of the expansion. Thus to replace the assumption in the standard model that the universe is infinite at each instant after the Big Bang, we are led to models in which the expansion emerges from an event that is more similar to a classical shock wave explosion, than it is to the usual scenario of the Big Bang.

In previous work, we constructed such models by matching FRW metrics to standard Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) metrics, (the metric for a static fluid sphere in general relativity), across a shock wave interface, [14, 21]. In that work we derived an upper limit on the distance that a shock wave could be from the FRW center, and this distance turned out to be closer than astronomical observations suggest it could be. (Astronomical observations currently extend out to approximately 1.51.5 Hubble lengths.) In this paper we begin by showing that this upper bound on the shock position that we identified in [21] for standard FRW-TOV shock matching, is exactly equal to one Hubble length. Indeed, we show that in order for the shock position to lie beyond one Hubble length in an FRW metric, it is necessary that the spacetime beyond the shock wave lie inside a Black Hole. Thus our previous shock matching limit of one Hubble length results from the fact that a standard TOV metric cannot be continued into a Black Hole, except in the special case when the pressure is zero, (we proved this in [15]). With this motivation, we here derive a new class of gravitational metrics that we call the TOV metric inside the Black Hole. (In contrast to the standard TOV metric, the TOV metric inside the Black Hole is dynamical.) Based on this, we develop a theory of FRW-TOV shock matching inside the Black Hole, and we use this to construct a new class of exact shock wave solutions of the Einstein equations, in which a shock wave is incorporated into the FRW metric at distances arbitrarily far beyond the Hubble length. This demonstrates that the limit in our previous work [21], that the shock position must lie within one Hubble length of the FRW center in FRW-TOV shock matching, can be overcome.

In the exact solutions constructed in this paper, the expanding FRW universe emerges behind a subluminous blast wave that explodes outward from the FRW origin r¯=0\bar{r}=0 at the instant of the Big Bang t=0,t=0,33 3 Here, r¯=R⁡(t)​r\bar{r}=R(t)r measures radial arclength distance at each fixed time tt in FRW coordinates, where R⁡(t)R(t) denotes the cosmological scale factor, and rr is the standard FRW radial coordinate, c.f. (2.4), (2.5) below. at a distance beyond one Hubble length44 4 The Hubble length c/H⁡(t)=[R˙​(t)c​R​(t)]−1c/H(t)=\left[\frac{\dot{R}(t)}{cR(t)}\right]^{-1} depends on the cosmological scale factor R⁡(t),R(t), and an easy calculation using the Einstein equations shows that in the FRW spacetime, the Hubble length increases with time. Thus more and more galaxies pass inside of the threshold distance of one Hubble length and come into view as time evolves. The Hubble length c/H0c/H_{0} at present time is estimated to be around 101010^{10} light years.. The distance of one Hubble length is critical in the FRW metric because the total FRW mass MM inside radius r¯\bar{r} satisfies 2​Mr¯<1,\frac{2M}{\bar{r}}<1, out to exactly one Hubble length. Thus, one Hubble length marks the event horizon of a Black Hole in a shock wave model in which the mass MM is isolated in an asymptotically Schwarzschild metric—the TOV metric in our model. (In contrast to the TOV metric outside the Black Hole, the TOV metric inside the Black Hole can be continued into an event horizon, c.f. the remarks after Theorem 6 below.) After the Big Bang, the shock wave in our exact solution continues to weaken as it expands outward, satisfying the entropy condition for shocks all the way out until the Hubble length eventually catches up to the shock wave 55 5 In our cosmological interpretation of the FRW metric, we (loosely) identify the motion of the galaxies with the motion of the FRW fluid, which is taken to be a perfect fluid with nonzero pressure, co-moving with the FRW metric. We show below that, although the shock wave moves outward through the galaxies, (r˙>0\dot{r}>0), and the Hubble length increases with time, the number of Hubble lengths from the FRW center to the shock wave, (c.f. (5.36) below), as well as the total mass behind the shock wave, both decrease in time in these exact solutions, tending to infinity in backwards time at the instant of the Big Bang. This is no contradiction because the FRW pressure pp is assumed nonzero, c.f. Corollary 1 below.. At this instant the shock wave lies at the critical distance of exactly one Hubble length from the FRW center. From this time onward, the shock wave can be approximated by a zero pressure, k=0k=0 Oppenheimer-Snyder (OS) interface that emerges from the White Hole event horizon of an ambient Schwarzschild metric of finite mass. (The entropy condition implies that the TOV density and pressure tend to zero as the shock interface approaches the critical distance of one Hubble length.) Thereafter the interface continues out to infinity along a geodesic of the Schwarzschild metric outside the Black Hole. Thus the OS solution gives the large time asymptotics of this new class of shock wave solutions that evolve inside a Black Hole.

One of the surprises in the analysis is that the equation of state that applies at the earliest stage of Big Bang physics, p=c23​ρ,p=\frac{c^{2}}{3}\rho, is distinguished by the equations, and only for this equation of state does the shock wave emerge from the Big Bang at a finite nonzero speed, the speed of light, decelerating to a subluminous wave from that time onward..

These new shock wave solutions of the Einstein equations confirm the mathematical consistency of an FRW universe of finite extent and non-zero pressure expanding outward from behind an entropy satisfying shock wave emerging from the origin at subluminous speed beyond one Hubble length at the instant of the Big Bang, a prerequisite for early Big Bang physics. Since the shock wave emerges from the Big Bang beyond one Hubble length, it would account for the thermalization of radiation in a region that is initially well beyond the light cone of an observer positioned at the FRW center. Thus our attempt to incorporate a shock wave beyond one Hubble length has led to unexpected and interesting connections between Big Bang Cosmology and Black Holes. But furthermore, we suggest that general relativity pretty much forces the qualitative behavior we see here into any reasonable model that relaxes the assumption in the standard model that the expansion of the galaxies is of infinite extent at each fixed time. (One could say that in these new models, the Copernican Principle is replaced by the principle in physics that Nothing Is Infinite.)

In Section 2 we transform the FRW metric to standard Schwarzschild coordinates, and use this to discuss the connection between the Hubble length and the Schwarzschild radius. In Section 3 we construct the extension of the zero pressure, k=0,k=0, OS solution to the interior of a Black Hole by using Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates to regularize the event horizon of the Schwarzschild metric, [9, 17]. We return to these OS solutions in Section 6 where we argue that the shock wave solutions constructed there continue naturally to the OS solution after the solution has relaxed to almost zero pressure.

In Section 4 we construct the TOV metric inside the Black Hole. We refer to this metric as TOV because the metric components depend only on the radial coordinate r¯,\bar{r}, but, as in the Schwarzschild metric, the TOV radial coordinate is timelike inside the Black Hole. It follows that the mass function MM is constant in each spacelike slice r¯=c​o​n​s​t.\bar{r}=const. of the TOV metric inside the Black Hole.

In Section 5 we develop the theory of shock matching between a k=0k=0 FRW metric and TOV metrics inside the Black Hole. The shock matching techniques introduced in [13] must be modified inside the Black Hole because the conservation constraint used in [13] introduces unphysical (characteristic) solutions. The analysis leads to the derivation of a system of differential equations that simultaneously describe the time evolution of the shock position together with the outer TOV pressure, and for solutions of these equations, the shock interface must lie beyond one Hubble length from the center in the FRW metric. One interesting feature of the matching is that the radial coordinate r¯\bar{r}, a timelike coordinate in the TOV metric, is identified through shock matching with the FRW spacelike coordinate r¯\bar{r} that measures radial arclength distance from the center at each fixed value of the (standard) time tt in the FRW metric. Another interesting feature is that the mass function M,M, which is continuous across shocks as a consequence of shock matching, has the physical interpretation as a total mass inside radius r¯\bar{r} in the FRW metric, but MM has no such interpretation in the TOV metric by itself, and in fact we know of no general physical interpretation of the mass function MM inside the Black Hole.

In Section 6 we formulate the entropy condition, and construct a class of global, entropy satisfying shock wave solutions of the Einstein equations under the simplifying assumption that the FRW sound speed σ\sqrt{\sigma} is constant, (that is, we assume the FRW equation of state p=σ​ρ,p=\sigma\rho, σ=c​o​n​s​t.>0\sigma=const.>0, c.f. [14]). This includes the important case σ=c23,\sigma=\frac{c^{2}}{3}, usually assumed at the earliest stage of Big Bang physics. (This is the equation of state in the extreme relativistic limit of free particles, and for pure radiation, [13].) Remarkably, under a change of variables, the shock matching equations of Section 5 reduce to a planar autonomous system when σ=c​o​n​s​t.,\sigma=const., and this system is amenable to global analysis, a requirement for the construction of solutions in the large. It is very interesting that the special value σ=c2/3\sigma=c^{2}/3 plays distinguished role, and at this unique value, the shock wave is everywhere subluminous after the Big Bang, but emerges from the Big Bang at exactly the speed of light. For all other values of σ,\sigma, we prove that the shock speed at the instant of the Big Bang is either zero, or infinite, and is everywhere subluminous if and only if σ≤c2/3.\sigma\leq c^{2}/3. This is surprising because the equation of state p=c23​ρp=\frac{c^{2}}{3}\rho played no special role in shock matching outside the Black Hole.

The class of exact solutions in Section 6 describes the global dynamics of an FRW universe of finite extent which explodes outward behind an entropy satisfying, subluminous shock wave, emerging from the origin, beyond one Hubble length, at the instant of the Big Bang. Because the TOV metric inside the Black Hole has nonzero density and pressure, it follows that, unlike the OS solutions of Section 3, these new exact shock wave solutions do not require any part of the empty space Schwarzschild solution inside the Black Hole for their construction. On the other hand, the fact that the OS solution gives the qualitative large time behavior of the solutions independent of σ,\sigma, (a consequence of the entropy condition alone), suggests that the qualitative features of these solutions may be generic for a large class of equations of state.

In Section 7 we obtain estimates for the shock position. The conclusion of Theorem 9 is this: Let t0t_{0} be the first time at which the shock becomes visible at the FRW center. In our exact solutions, we assume the FRW equation of state p=σ​ρ,p=\sigma\rho, σ=c​o​n​s​t,\sigma=const, 0<σ≤1/3.0<\sigma\leq 1/3. (We use the convention that we take c=1c=1 when convenient.) For these solutions, the shock wave will first become visible at the center r¯=0\bar{r}=0 of the FRW spacetime at FRW time t=t0,t=t_{0}, at the moment when the Hubble length satisfies

1H⁡(t0)=1+3​σ2​r∗,\displaystyle\frac{1}{H(t_{0})}=\frac{1+3\sigma}{2}r_{*}, (1.1)

where r∗r_{*} is the FRW position of the shock at the instant of the Big Bang. (The actual arclength distance from the center to the shock at the Big Bang will be r¯=0.\bar{r}=0. ) At this time, the number of Hubble lengths N0\sqrt{N}_{0} from the FRW center to the shock wave at time t=t0t=t_{0} satisfies the bounds

Thus, in particular, the shock wave will still lie beyond one Hubble length at the FRW time t0t_{0} when it first becomes visible. We conclude in these shock wave cosmological models, that at the moment t∗t_{*} when the shock wave first becomes visible at the FRW center, it must lie within 4.5 Hubble lengths of the center. Throughout the expansion up until this time, the expanding universe must lie entirely within a Black Hole—the universe will eventually emerge from this Black Hole, but not until some later time tc​r​i​t,t_{crit}, where tc​r​i​tt_{crit} does not exceed 3​t∗.3t_{*}.

Concluding remarks are made in the final section.

2 The Hubble Distance and the Schwarzschild Radius

According to Einstein’s Theory of General Relativity, all properties of the gravitational field are determined by a Lorentzian spacetime metric tensor g,g, whose line element in a given coordinate system x=(x0,…,x3)x=(x^{0},...,x^{3}) is given by

d​s2=gi​j​d​xi​d​xj.ds^{2}=g_{ij}dx^{i}dx^{j}. (2.1)

(We use the Einstein summation convention whereby all repeated up-down indices are assumed summed from 00 to 3.3.) The components gi​jg_{ij} of the gravitational metric gg satisfy the Einstein equations,

Gi​j=κ​Ti​j,Ti​j=(ρ​c2+p)​wi​wj+p​gi​j,G^{ij}=\kappa T^{ij},\ \ \ T^{ij}=(\rho c^{2}+p)w^{i}w^{j}+pg^{ij}, (2.2)

where we assume the stress-energy tensor TT of a perfect fluid. Here GG is the Einstein curvature tensor,

κ=8​π​𝒢c4\kappa=\frac{8\pi{\cal G}}{c^{4}} (2.3)

is the coupling constant, 𝒢{\cal G} is Newton’s gravitational constant, cc is the speed of light, ρ​c2\rho c^{2} is the energy density, pp is the pressure, and 𝐰=(w0,…,w3){\bf w}=(w^{0},...,w^{3}) are the components of the 44-velocity of the fluid, c.f. [24]. We use the convention that we take c=1c=1 and 𝒢=1{\cal G}=1 when convenient.

In this section we consider the FRW metric, a spacetime metric whose line element takes the form

d​s2=−d​t2+R​(t)2​(d​r21−k​r2+r2​d​Ω2),ds^{2}=-dt^{2}+R(t)^{2}\left(\frac{dr^{2}}{1-kr^{2}}+r^{2}d\Omega^{2}\right), (2.4)

where R⁡(t)R(t) is the so-called cosmological scale factor, and d​Ω2=d​θ2+s​i​n2​θ​d​ϕ2d\Omega^{2}=d\theta^{2}+sin^{2}\theta d\phi^{2} denotes the line element on the unit 2-sphere. The FRW metric describes the time evolution of a three dimensional space of constant scalar curvature, (the tt=const. surfaces), and kk can be assumed to take one of the values {−1,0,1}\{-1,0,1\} via a rescaling of the radial coordinate r.r. Radial distance at each fixed time in the FRW metric is measured by r¯,\bar{r}, where

r¯=R⁡(t)​r,\bar{r}=R(t)r, (2.5)

and it is standard to rescale time so that RR goes from 00 to 1,1, where R=0,R=0, t=0t=0 corresponds to the Big Bang, and R=1,R=1, t=t0t=t_{0} corresponds to present time.

The Hubble constant H,H, (which actually depends on tt), is given in terms of R⁡(t)R(t) by

H≡H⁡(t)=R˙​(t)R⁡(t),H\equiv H(t)=\frac{\dot{R}(t)}{R(t)}, (2.6)

and we let H0=H⁡(t0)H_{0}=H(t_{0}) denote the present value of the Hubble constant.

The Hubble length c/Hc/H, (the reciprocal of the Hubble constant when we take c=1c=1), gives a length scale determined by the expansion rate of the galaxies, and can be interpreted as the travel distance for a light ray starting at the Big Bang and ending at time t.t. (That is, the age of the universe is approximately H0−1≈1010H_{0}^{-1}\approx 10^{10} years, so the Hubble length c/H0≈1010c/H_{0}\approx 10^{10} light years, is a measure of the distance light travels during this time interval, [24].) The Hubble length is thus a measure of the distance to the furthest objects that can be seen in the universe at a given time. (Estimates for this distance in terms of radial arclength r¯\bar{r} at fixed FRW time tt are given in Theorems 1 and 2 below.)

Putting the metric ansatz (2.4) into the Einstein equations (2.2) gives the equations for the FRW metric, [24],

H2=(R˙R)2=κ3​ρ−kR2,H^{2}=\left(\frac{\dot{R}}{R}\right)^{2}=\frac{\kappa}{3}\rho-\frac{k}{R^{2}}, (2.7)

and

ρ˙=−3​(p+ρ)​H.\dot{\rho}=-3(p+\rho)H. (2.8)

The unknowns R,R, ρ\rho and pp are assumed to be functions of the FRW coordinate time tt alone, and “dot” denotes differentiation with respect to t.t. In this paper, we focus on the case of critical expansion, the case k=0,k=0, [1, 24].

When k=0,k=0, the t=c​o​n​s​t.t=const. surfaces in the FRW metric are infinite, flat, Euclidean 33-space. It follows that the standard model of cosmology based on a critically expanding FRW metric, [1], implicitly assumes that the expansion rate HH of the universe is constant all the way out to infinity at each fixed time tt in the FRW metric—this even though, based on lookback time, we can in principle only observe the universe out to about 101010^{10} light years.

If, on the other hand, there is a shock wave at the leading edge of the expansion of the galaxies, then the following question presents itself: What is the critical radius r¯c​r​i​t\bar{r}_{crit} at each fixed time tt in a k=0k=0 FRW metric such that the total mass inside a shock wave positioned beyond that radius puts the universe inside a Black Hole? Indeed, there must always be such a critical radius because the total mass M⁡(r¯,t)M(\bar{r},t) inside radius r¯\bar{r} in the FRW metric at fixed time tt increases like r¯3,\bar{r}^{3}, and so at each fixed time tt we must have r¯>2​M​(r¯,t)\bar{r}>2M(\bar{r},t) for small enough r¯,\bar{r}, while the reverse inequality holds for large r¯.\bar{r}. Thus for every time tt there must exist a smallest r¯=r¯c​r​i​t\bar{r}=\bar{r}_{crit} for which r¯c​r​i​t=2​M​(r¯c​r​i​t,t).\bar{r}_{crit}=2M(\bar{r}_{crit},t). This critical radius then marks the Schwarzschild radius in the metric that lies beyond the shock wave when it is at that position. We will presently show that when k=0,k=0, r¯c​r​i​t\bar{r}_{crit} equals the Hubble length, and this explains the shock matching limit uncovered in our previous work in terms of the Hubble length, (c.f. Section 6, [21]). That is, we cannot match a critically expanding FRW metric to a classical TOV metric beyond one Hubble length without continuing the TOV solution into a Black Hole—and we showed in [15] that the standard TOV metric cannot be continued into a Black Hole.

At this point we make a note on terminology: we say that a radial solution of the Einstein equations is inside the Black Hole provided that 2​Mr¯>1.\frac{2M}{\bar{r}}>1. If further, the radial coordinate r¯\bar{r} is always increasing along timelike curves, then we also refer to such a region 2​Mr¯>1\frac{2M}{\bar{r}}>1 as a White Hole, but we will nevertheless use the term Black Hole whenever 2​Mr¯>1.\frac{2M}{\bar{r}}>1.. For example, in the Kruskal development of a Schwarzschild Black Hole there are four quadrants, and one quadrant contains the Black Hole singularity and the opposite quadrant, (its time reversal), contains the White Hole singularity, [9]. Both quadrants lie within the region where 2​Mr¯>1,\frac{2M}{\bar{r}}>1, and the quadrant with the Black [resp. White] Hole singularity at r¯=0\bar{r}=0 has the property that all timelike geodesics end [resp. begin] at the singularity in finite proper time66 6 By itself, Einstein’s theory is time reversible, the direction of forward time is left undetermined, and extra conditions like entropy conditions for shocks are needed to determine the direction of forward time. In the region 2​M/r¯>12M/\bar{r}>1 outside the event horizon, the Schwarzschild metric is symmetric under time reversal in the sense that the time reversal of a geodesic remains a geodesic. However in the region 2​M/r¯<1,2M/\bar{r}<1, the time reversal of the Schwarzschild metric takes the Black Hole region beyond t=+∞t=+\infty to the White Hole region before t=−∞t=-\infty. Thus without extra conditions, the expanding White Hole is just as admissible a solution of the Einstein equations as is its time reversal, the collapsing Black Hole.. Thus if r¯c​r​i​t=c/H,\bar{r}_{crit}=c/H, and the mass function MM is continuous across shock waves, (both of which we demonstrate below), then it follows that one can incorporate a shock wave into an FRW metric beyond one Hubble length only if the metric beyond the shock wave lies inside a Black Hole, where 2​M​(r¯,t)r¯>1.\frac{2M(\bar{r},t)}{\bar{r}}>1.

We now verify that r¯c​r​i​t=c/H,\bar{r}_{crit}=c/H, and that the Hubble length is the limit for FRW-TOV shock matching outside a Black Hole, c.f. [21]. To this end, write the FRW metric (2.4) in standard Schwarzschild coordinates 𝐱¯=(r¯,t¯){\bf\bar{x}}=(\bar{r},\bar{t}) where the metric takes the form

d​s2=−B⁡(r¯,t¯)​d​t¯2+A​(r¯,t¯)−1​d​r¯2+r¯2​d​Ω2,ds^{2}=-B(\bar{r},\bar{t})d\bar{t}^{2}+A(\bar{r},\bar{t})^{-1}d\bar{r}^{2}+\bar{r}^{2}d\Omega^{2}, (2.9)

and the mass function M⁡(r¯,t¯)M(\bar{r},\bar{t}) is defined through the relation

A=1−2​Mr¯.\displaystyle A=1-\frac{2M}{\bar{r}}. (2.10)

(We have set 𝒢=c=1,{\cal G}=c=1, and our notation is to denote the standard, non-angular FRW coordinates by 𝐱=(x0,x1)=(t,r),{\bf x}=(x^{0},x^{1})=(t,r), but TOV coordinates are denoted by 𝐱¯=(x¯0,x¯1)=(r¯,t¯){\bf\bar{x}}=(\bar{x}^{0},\bar{x}^{1})=(\bar{r},\bar{t}) because we work inside the Black Hole where A<0A<0 and r¯\bar{r} is the timelike coordinate.) d​r=d​r¯R−r¯R2​R˙​d​t.dr=\frac{d\bar{r}}{R}-\frac{\bar{r}}{R^{2}}\dot{R}dt.

Using this in the FRW line element we find

d​s2=−C​d​t2+D​d​r¯2+2​E​d​r¯​d​t+r¯2​d​Ω2,ds^{2}=-Cdt^{2}+Dd\bar{r}^{2}+2Ed\bar{r}dt+\bar{r}^{2}d\Omega^{2}, (2.11)

where

d​t¯=(ψ​C)​d​t−(ψ​E)​d​r¯,\displaystyle d\bar{t}=(\psi C)dt-(\psi E)d\bar{r}, (2.15)

d​s2=−1C​ψ2​d​t¯2+(D+E2C)​d​r¯2+r¯2​d​Ω2.ds^{2}=-\frac{1}{C\psi^{2}}d\bar{t}^{2}+\left(D+\frac{E^{2}}{C}\right)d\bar{r}^{2}+\bar{r}^{2}d\Omega^{2}. (2.17)

d​s2=−1ψ2​{1−k​r21−k​r2−H2​r¯2}​d​t¯2+{11−k​r2−H2​r¯2}​d​r¯2+r¯2​d​Ω2.ds^{2}=-\frac{1}{\psi^{2}}\left\{\frac{1-kr^{2}}{1-kr^{2}-H^{2}\bar{r}^{2}}\right\}d\bar{t}^{2}+\left\{\frac{1}{1-kr^{2}-H^{2}\bar{r}^{2}}\right\}d\bar{r}^{2}+\bar{r}^{2}d\Omega^{2}. (2.18)

3 The OS Solution Inside the Black Hole

The simplest model of a localized FRW metric contained within a shock boundary that lies beyond the Hubble distance, is one in which p≡0,p\equiv 0, and the FRW metric is matched to the Schwarzschild metric at a contact discontinuity interface positioned inside the Black Hole of the Schwarzschild metric. This poses the problem of extending the OS solution smoothly into the interior of a Schwarzschild Black Hole. In this section we construct the OS solution inside the Black Hole in the case k=0,k=0, making the point of discussing it from the FRW point of view, in terms of the Hubble length. (See [10] and [9] for a discussion of the case k<0.k<0.) The k=0k=0 OS solution inside the Black Hole will give us a point of comparison for the p≠0p\neq 0 shock wave models constructed in Sections 5 and 6, and we argue in Section 7 that the (expanding) OS solution also describes the large time asymptotics of these shock wave models. When p≠0,p\neq 0, the resulting interface is a shock wave, and an entropy condition breaks the time symmetry. In our examples of Section 6, it is the outward expanding solution (explosion) that globally meets the entropy condition, (not the inward collapse), thus making the cosmological interpretation of the model relevant. In contrast, the interface in the OS solution is time reversible, but the collapsing solution is the one that is relevant in the standard interpretation of the OS solution as a pressureless sphere collapsing into a Black Hole, [10, 9].

Our method is to match the k=0k=0 FRW metric to the empty space Schwarzschild metric written in Eddington-Finkelstein (EF) coordinates [9], across a shock interface77 7 The interface in the OS solutions is, in the language of gas dynamics, a contact discontinuity, which is time reversible because neither mass nor momentum cross the interface. that lies beyond the Hubble length on the FRW side of the shock. As in a classical explosion, we assume that the FRW metric lies inside a bounded region behind an outgoing shock interface, and for the OS solution we assume that the Schwarzschild metric describes the spacetime beyond the interface. Thus in the OS model, the shock wave (contact discontinuity) marks the leading edge of the expansion of the FRW metric.

The EF coordinates provide a regularization of the Schwarzschild metric at the event horizon, and the mapping from the EF spacetime to the Schwarzschild spacetime is a 1-1 mapping, [9]. Both coordinate systems cover the region of the Schwarzschild metric outside the event horizon, together with that portion of the Black Hole that is coordinatized by the Schwarzschild coordinates. Here, since we are dealing with an expanding FRW solution, we work with the time reversal of these metrics, which covers the region beyond the event horizon, together with the White Hole region inside the Black Hole We show that with this latter time orientation, we can match the EF metric to the spacetime described by a critically expanding FRW metric across a discontinuity at finite radius, and its time reversal provides the corresponding matching to the critically contracting FRW metric.

We return to these OS solutions in Section 6 where we argue that the shock wave solutions constructed there continue naturally to the OS solution after the TOV density and pressure tend to zero, assuming that the shock has relaxed to a sufficiently weak wave. But we find this OS model interesting in its own right because it not only provides the simplest model in which the expansion of the galaxies corresponds to the expansion of a finite total mass with a wave at the leading edge of the expansion, but it also embeds the Big Bang singularity of an FRW metric within the singularity of a larger spacetime—the larger spacetime being the empty space Schwarzschild solution, and its singularity being the White Hole singularity that lies inside the event horizon in the Kruskal development of the Schwarzschild metric. Such an embedding is possible only under the assumption that the Hubble law applies to a bounded region of spacetime, because the infinite FRW metric cannot be matched to the Schwarzschild metric.

In EF coordinates, the Schwarzschild line element takes the form

d​s^2=−A​d​t^2−2​d​r¯​d​t^+r¯2​d​Ω2,\displaystyle d\hat{s}^{2}=-Ad\hat{t}^{2}-2d\bar{r}d\hat{t}+\bar{r}^{2}d\Omega^{2}, (3.1)

where

A=1−2​Mr¯,\displaystyle A=1-\frac{2M}{\bar{r}}, (3.2)

and MM is the constant mass of the Schwarzschild solution. Indeed, using (2.11)-(2.16), the time coordinate t¯\bar{t} that eliminates the mixed term in (3.1) satisfies

d​t¯=ψ​A​d​t^−ψ​r¯,\displaystyle d\bar{t}=\psi Ad\hat{t}-\psi\bar{r}, (3.3)

where ψ\psi satisfies

∂∂t^​ψ+∂∂r¯​(ψ​A)=0.\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial\hat{t}}\psi+\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{r}}(\psi A)=0. (3.4)

The solution to (3.3), (3.4) is

ψ=1/A,\displaystyle\psi=1/A, (3.5)
t¯=t−r¯−l​n​|r¯−2​G​M|,\displaystyle\bar{t}=t-\bar{r}-ln|\bar{r}-2GM|, (3.6)

and in (r¯,t¯)(\bar{r},\bar{t})-coordinates the metric takes the standard Schwarzschild form

d​s2=−A​d​t¯2+1A​d​r¯2+r¯2​d​Ω2.\displaystyle ds^{2}=-Ad\bar{t}^{2}+\frac{1}{A}d\bar{r}^{2}+\bar{r}^{2}d\Omega^{2}. (3.7)

Thus (3.6) defines a 1−11-1 mapping (t^,r¯)→(r¯,t¯)(\hat{t},\bar{r})\rightarrow(\bar{r},\bar{t}) taking {r¯>2M}×𝐑\left\{\bar{r}>2M\right\}\times{\bf R} to itself, and another 1−11-1 mapping (t^,r¯)→(r¯,t¯)(\hat{t},\bar{r})\rightarrow(\bar{r},\bar{t}) taking {0<r¯<2M}×𝐑\left\{0<\bar{r}<2M\right\}\times{\bf R} to itself. This verifies the claim that the EF metric covers two of the four quadrants of the (maximal) Kruskal development of the Schwarzschild metric in a 1−11-1 fashion. Unlike the Schwarzschild metric, the EF metric is smooth at r¯=2​M,\bar{r}=2M, and this is reflected in the singularity of the transformation (3.6) at r¯=2​M.\bar{r}=2M. Note that in (r¯,t¯)(\bar{r},\bar{t}) coordinates, the vector field ∂∂r¯\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{r}} is timelike, spacelike, when r¯<2​M,\bar{r}<2M, r¯>2​M,\bar{r}>2M, respectively; while in (t^,r¯)(\hat{t},\bar{r}) coordinates, the vector field ∂∂r¯\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{r}} is lightlike. This is no contradiction because ∂∂r¯\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{r}} points along the level curves of its complementary coordinates in a given coordinate system. On the other hand, the vector fields ∂∂t¯\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{t}} and ∂∂t^\frac{\partial}{\partial\hat{t}} both point along the level curves of r¯,\bar{r}, and hence retain the same character as spacelike or timelike according to the sign of A.A.

Since k=0k=0 and p=0,p=0, the FRW equations (2.7), (2.8) imply

H2=κ3​ρ.\displaystyle H^{2}=\frac{\kappa}{3}\rho. (3.20)

Using (3.20) and (3.2) together with ϕ2=1\phi^{2}=1 in (3.19) yields the equation for the shock surface,

M=κ6​ρ​(t)​r¯3.\displaystyle M=\frac{\kappa}{6}\rho(t)\bar{r}^{3}. (3.21)

Solving (3.21) for r¯\bar{r} as a function of tt gives the shock surface r¯=r¯​(t)\bar{r}=\bar{r}(t) in the FRW coordinate. It follows from the FRW equations (2.7), (2.8) in the case p=0,p=0, that R​(t)3​ρ​(t)R(t)^{3}\rho(t) is constant on FRW solutions, [24]. Using this in (3.21) implies that r=r0=c​o​n​s​t.r=r_{0}=const. describes the interface in the OS solution. For example, if we choose R⁡(t0)=1R(t_{0})=1 at present time t=t0,t=t_{0}, then

r0={6​Mκ​ρ​(t0)}1/3\displaystyle r_{0}=\left\{\frac{6M}{\kappa\rho(t_{0})}\right\}^{1/3} (3.22)

is constant on the interface, and thus r¯​(t)=R​(t)​r0\bar{r}(t)=R(t)r_{0} describes the motion of the interface in the OS solution. The fact that r=c​o​n​s​t.r=const. along the interface implies that the interface moves with the galaxies of the p=0p=0 FRW metric, and hence neither mass nor momentum crosses the interface. From this we can also see that the shock surface is non-characteristic for the PDE (3.11). Indeed, the characteristic curves for (3.11) satisfy

d​r¯d​t=−1b=(R˙​r0)−+​1,\frac{d\bar{r}}{dt}=-\frac{1}{b}=(\dot{R}r_{0})^{+}_{-}1,

on the shock surface, where the +−{}^{+}_{-} agrees with the sign of R˙.\dot{R}. Thus we see that d​r¯d​t=(R˙​r0)−+​1\frac{d\bar{r}}{dt}=(\dot{R}r_{0})^{+}_{-}1 along the characteristic, and d​r¯d​t=R˙​r0\frac{d\bar{r}}{dt}=\dot{R}r_{0} along the shock surface, so the two can never be equal. We conclude that the shock surface is never characteristic for equation (3.11), and hence ϕ,\phi, as well as the coordinate t^,\hat{t}, can be defined in a neighborhood of the interface.

Note that the shock surface equation (3.21) tells us that r¯\bar{r} goes from zero to infinity as the FRW density goes from infinity to zero. For example in the case R˙>0,\dot{R}>0, this tells us that the FRW universe starts at the White Hole singularity of the EF metric at the instant t=0t=0 of the Big Bang. From this time onward, the shock surface r¯​(t)=(6​Mκ​ρ​(t))1/3\bar{r}(t)=\left(\frac{6M}{\kappa\rho(t)}\right)^{1/3} continues out until the the Hubble distance H−1=(3κ​ρ​(t))1/2,H^{-1}=\left(\frac{3}{\kappa\rho(t)}\right)^{1/2}, (c.f. (3.20)), catches up to the shock surface on the FRW side of the shock, which happens at the FRW time tst_{s} when r¯​(ts)=2​M,\bar{r}(t_{s})=2M, i.e., when the shock surface lies on the event horizon of the outer EF metric. As the FRW time increases from tst_{s} to ∞,\infty, the interface continues on out to infinity, staying inside the Hubble length on the FRW side of the shock, and outside the Black Hole on the EF side.

Note also that the coordinate r¯\bar{r} is a spacelike coordinate that measures arc-length distance in the FRW metric at fixed time tt in the FRW coordinate system (t,r¯)(t,\bar{r}) on the FRW side of the shock, but on the EF side of the shock, the coordinate r¯\bar{r} is lightlike in E​FEF coordinates (t^,r¯),(\hat{t},\bar{r}), and changes from timelike to spacelike in standard Schwarzschild coordinates (r¯,t¯)(\bar{r},\bar{t}) as the shock surface passes through the event horizon of the EF metric—even so, the coordinate identification (t,r)→(t^,r¯)(t,r)\rightarrow(\hat{t},\bar{r}) is regular in a neighborhood of the shock surface for all shock positions 0<r¯<∞.0<\bar{r}<\infty. This is no contradiction, because the coordinate vector field ∂∂r¯\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{r}} remains undetermined until a choice of complementary coordinate is specified.

In conclusion, we have that the interface between the FRW and Schwarzschild metrics in the k=0k=0 OS solution is a contact discontinuity that traverses a geodesic of the Schwarzschild metric. The total mass of the FRW metric behind the shock wave interface is finite and constant in time, and emerges from the White Hole singularity of the ambient Schwarzschild metric at r¯=0,\bar{r}=0, the instant of the Big Bang. After a finite proper time, the solution continues out through the event horizon at Schwarzschild time t=−∞,t=-\infty, and continues to expand forever into the asymptotically flat Schwarzshild spacetime outside the Black Hole, where 2​Mr¯<1.\frac{2M}{\bar{r}}<1. In this regime the solution agrees with the k=0k=0 OS solution given in [17]88 8 It is well known that the spacetime coordinatized by either the EF or Schwarzschild coordinates is not a geodesically complete spacetime. That is, from the point of view of the (complete) Kruskal development of the Schwarzschild spacetime, the EF metric covers only two of the four quadrants determined by the event horizon in the Kruskal diagram; namely, the standard quadrant outside the Black Hole together with the quadrant which contains the Black Hole singularity–or else under time reversal, the standard quadrant outside the Black Hole together with the region containing the White Hole singularity. On the other hand, the OS solution is a geodesically complete spacetime because, from the Kruskal point of view, it consists of the Schwarzschild solution on one side, and the FRW solution on the other side, of the geodesic defined by the trajectory of the interface of discontinuity. Thus, by removing a neighborhood of either the White Hole or the Black Hole event horizon, the OS matching also eliminates the incomplete geodesics that emerge from t=−∞,t=-\infty, respectively t=+∞,t=+\infty,, depending on the time orientation of the solution, [9]..

4 The TOV Solution Inside the Black Hole

The standard Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) metric models a static fluid sphere in general relativity. It was proved in [15] that the standard TOV metric for a static fluid sphere, by itself, does not admit Black Holes, and can only exist when 2​Mr¯<1.\frac{2M}{\bar{r}}<1. In this section we derive the equations for the analogue of the TOV solution inside the Black Hole.

The TOV solutions inside the Black Hole are used in Sections 5 and 6 to extend the OS solution of Section 3 to the case of non-zero pressure, inside the Black Hole. When p≠0,p\neq 0, energy and momentum cross the interface, and so the contact discontinuity of the OS solution must be replaced by a shock wave discontinuity. Thus in order to extend our shock matching techniques beyond the Hubble length when p≠0,p\neq 0, we must replace the outer Schwarzschild metric of the OS solution with a metric that contains matter, and satisfies 2​M/r¯>1.2M/\bar{r}>1. The TOV metric inside the Black Hole is the simplest metric that satisfies these conditions. We refer to it as TOV because the components depend only on the radial coordinate r¯,\bar{r}, as in the standard TOV metric, but now r¯\bar{r} is timelike. (As in the Schwarzschild metric, the roles of space and time are interchanged inside the Black Hole.) In shock matching with FRW metrics, this new TOV metric inside the Black Hole will play the role of a transitional solution that mediates the mass flux across the shock interface during the time after the Big Bang when the densities are large, and up until the time when the solution has settled down to a zero pressure OS expansion.

The usual ansatz for a TOV metric takes the form

d​s2=−B​d​t¯2+A−1​d​r¯2+r¯2​d​Ω2,\displaystyle ds^{2}=-Bd\bar{t}^{2}+A^{-1}d\bar{r}^{2}+\bar{r}^{2}d\Omega^{2}, (4.1)

where A⁡(r¯)A(\bar{r}) and B⁡(r¯)B(\bar{r}) depend only on the coordinate r¯.\bar{r}. Here

A⁡(r¯)=1−2​M​(r¯)r¯,\displaystyle A(\bar{r})=1-\frac{2M(\bar{r})}{\bar{r}}, (4.2)

and when r¯>2​M,\bar{r}>2M, M⁡(r¯)M(\bar{r}) has the interpretation as the total mass inside the ball of radius r¯.\bar{r}. Thus our assumption that the TOV metric lies inside the Black Hole or inside the Schwarzschild radius is equivalent to the assumption that

A<0.A<0.

We now obtain the Einstein equations for a perfect fluid under the assumption that the fluid is co-moving with respect to a metric of form (4.1), assuming that AA and BB depend only on r¯,\bar{r}, but now assuming that A<0.A<0. The stress tensor for a perfect fluid takes the form,

Ti​j=(ρ¯+p¯)​w¯i​w¯j+p¯​g¯i​j,\displaystyle T_{ij}=(\bar{\rho}+\bar{p})\bar{w}_{i}\bar{w}_{j}+\bar{p}\bar{g}_{ij}, (4.3)

and since r¯\bar{r} is the timelike coordinate for the TOV metric in (r¯,t¯)(\bar{r},\bar{t})-coordinates when A<0,A<0, the assumption that the fluid is co-moving with the TOV metric inside the Black Hole implies that, c.f. [24],

(w¯0,w¯1,w¯2,w¯3)=(w¯r¯,w¯t¯,w¯θ,w¯ϕ)=(1−A,0,0,0).\displaystyle(\bar{w}_{0},\bar{w}_{1},\bar{w}_{2},\bar{w}_{3})=(\bar{w}_{\bar{r}},\bar{w}_{\bar{t}},\bar{w}_{\theta},\bar{w}_{\phi})=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{-A}},0,0,0\right). (4.4)

In this case we obtain

T00≡Tr¯​r¯=(ρ¯+p¯)​(1−A)+p¯​(1A)=−ρ¯A,\displaystyle T_{00}\equiv T_{\bar{r}\bar{r}}=(\bar{\rho}+\bar{p})\left(\frac{1}{-A}\right)+\bar{p}\left(\frac{1}{A}\right)=-\frac{\bar{\rho}}{A}, (4.5)

and

T11≡Tt¯​t¯=p¯​g¯11=−p¯​B.\displaystyle T_{11}\equiv T_{\bar{t}\bar{t}}=\bar{p}\bar{g}_{11}=-\bar{p}B. (4.6)

Using MAPLE we find,

G00≡Gr¯​r¯=−r¯​A​B′−B+A​Br¯​A​B,\displaystyle G_{00}\equiv G_{\bar{r}\bar{r}}=-\frac{\bar{r}AB^{\prime}-B+AB}{\bar{r}AB}, (4.7)
G11≡Gt¯​t¯=−Br¯2​{r¯​A′−1+A}.\displaystyle G_{11}\equiv G_{\bar{t}\bar{t}}=-\frac{B}{\bar{r}^{2}}\left\{\bar{r}A^{\prime}-1+A\right\}. (4.8)

From (4.5)-(4.8), the Einstein equations G00=κ​T00G_{00}=\kappa T_{00} and G11=κ​T11G_{11}=\kappa T_{11} reduce to

B′B=1r¯​(1−AA)+κ​ρ¯A,\displaystyle\frac{B^{\prime}}{B}=\frac{1}{\bar{r}}\left(\frac{1-A}{A}\right)+\kappa\frac{\bar{\rho}}{A}, (4.9)

and

A′=1−Ar¯+κ​p¯​r¯,\displaystyle A^{\prime}=\frac{1-A}{\bar{r}}+\kappa\bar{p}\bar{r}, (4.10)

respectively.99 9 Beware that MAPLE’s convention is that −GM​A​P​L​E=G,-G_{MAPLE}=G, so the Einstein equations are −GM​A​P​L​E=κ​T.-G_{MAPLE}=\kappa T. From [24], equation (5.45), we also have

−p¯′=(p¯+ρ¯)​dd​r¯​ln⁡{1−A},\displaystyle-\bar{p}^{\prime}=(\bar{p}+\bar{\rho})\frac{d}{d\bar{r}}\ln\left\{\frac{1}{\sqrt{-A}}\right\}, (4.11)

which simplifies to

p¯′=p¯+ρ¯2​A′A=p¯+ρ¯2​A​{1−Ar¯+κ​p¯​r¯}.\displaystyle\bar{p}^{\prime}=\frac{\bar{p}+\bar{\rho}}{2}\frac{A^{\prime}}{A}=\frac{\bar{p}+\bar{\rho}}{2A}\left\{\frac{1-A}{\bar{r}}+\kappa\bar{p}\bar{r}\right\}. (4.12)

Using (4.2), we obtain the system

p¯′\displaystyle\bar{p}^{\prime} =\displaystyle= p¯+ρ¯2​A′A=p¯+ρ¯2​A​{1−Ar¯+κ​p¯​r¯},\displaystyle\frac{\bar{p}+\bar{\rho}}{2}\frac{A^{\prime}}{A}=\frac{\bar{p}+\bar{\rho}}{2A}\left\{\frac{1-A}{\bar{r}}+\kappa\bar{p}\bar{r}\right\}, (4.13)
A′\displaystyle A^{\prime} =\displaystyle= 1−Ar¯+κ​p¯​r¯,\displaystyle\frac{1-A}{\bar{r}}+\kappa\bar{p}\bar{r}, (4.14)
B′B\displaystyle\frac{B^{\prime}}{B} =\displaystyle= 1r¯​(1−AA)+κ​ρ¯A.\displaystyle\frac{1}{\bar{r}}\left(\frac{1-A}{A}\right)+\kappa\frac{\bar{\rho}}{A}. (4.15)

Alternatively, using the unknown N=1−AN=1-A instead of A,A, (a variable convenient for our subsequent analysis), we obtain the equivalent system,

p¯′\displaystyle\bar{p}^{\prime} =\displaystyle= p¯+ρ¯2​N′N−1,\displaystyle\frac{\bar{p}+\bar{\rho}}{2}\frac{N^{\prime}}{N-1}, (4.16)
N′\displaystyle N^{\prime} =\displaystyle= −{Nr¯+κ​p¯​r¯},\displaystyle-\left\{\frac{N}{\bar{r}}+\kappa\bar{p}\bar{r}\right\}, (4.17)
B′B\displaystyle\frac{B^{\prime}}{B} =\displaystyle= −1N−1​{Nr¯+κ​ρ¯}.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{N-1}\left\{\frac{N}{\bar{r}}+\kappa\bar{\rho}\right\}. (4.18)

Note that the essential reason why the equations for the TOV metric inside the Black Hole take a different form than the standard TOV equations “outside the Black Hole”, is that the assumption of co-moving puts the nonzero component of 𝐰{\bf w} on the timelike coordinate r¯\bar{r} when A<0,A<0, and on the timelike coordinate t¯\bar{t} when A>0.A>0. We conclude that system (4.16)-(4.18) defines a new class of gravitational metrics which describe spacetimes that evolve inside the Black Hole.

The TOV equations inside the Black Hole describe a time dependent metric in which the metric components, together with the fluid variables, are constant at each fixed value of the TOV timelike coordinate r¯.\bar{r}. Like the FRW metric, the TOV metric inside the Black Hole describes a fluid with pressure that emerges from a White Hole singularity at r¯=0,\bar{r}=0, the instant of the Big Bang, with one important difference: unlike the FRW metric, for the TOV metric inside the Black Hole, the total mass is constant on each spacelike slice r¯=c​o​n​s​t​a​n​t.\bar{r}=constant. In the next section we match the TOV metric inside the Black Hole to k=0k=0 FRW metrics across shock interfaces in order to make the expanding FRW universe finite, in the sense that the total mass on each spacelike hypersurface is finite.

5 Shock Matching Inside the Black Hole

In this section we derive the equations that describe the matching of a general k=0k=0 FRW metric to a TOV metric inside the Black Hole, at a shock wave interface across which energy and momentum are conserved. The equations, given in system (5.35)-(5.36) below, describe the simultaneous time evolution of the shock position together with the TOV metric inside the Black Hole such that the resulting metric matches a given k=0k=0 FRW metric Lipschitz continuously across the shock, and such that conservation of energy and momentum hold at the shock. The conservation constraint, given in (5.25) below, determines the TOV pressure, and this is used to close the equations, c.f [14]. Equations (5.35)-(5.36) then determine all other unknowns in the TOV metric beyond the shock, and guarantee conservation, once the FRW metric is assigned. In particular, the equations guarantee that there are no delta function sources produced by the (second order) Einstein equations due to the lower order smoothness (Lipschitz continuity) of the metrics at the shock, c.f. (i)-(iv) below. The success of the method relies on the fact that once Lipschitz continuity is imposed, the single conservation condition (5.25) alone guarantees the two conservation constraints of the Rankine-Hugoniot jump conditions at the shock, c.f. [13], and Theorem 3 below.

Solutions of equations (5.35)-(5.36) are formally time-reversible without the imposition of an entropy condition. In the next section we formulate an entropy condition that agrees with the entropy condition of gas dynamics, and we use this to construct exact solutions of (5.35)-(5.36) that describe a class of time-irreversible entropy satisfying shocks in which the TOV density and pressure satisfy the physical bounds 0<p¯<ρ¯.0<\bar{p}<\bar{\rho}.

To model the expanding universe with a spherical shock wave at FRW position r¯=r¯​(t),\bar{r}=\bar{r}(t), we assume that the FRW metric lies in the region r¯<r¯​(t),\bar{r}<\bar{r}(t), and the TOV metric lies beyond the shock wave at r¯>r¯​(t).\bar{r}>\bar{r}(t). The corresponding matching for a standard TOV metric outside the Black Hole, (and inside the Hubble length), was accomplished in [14, 15, 21]. In this section we do not use an EF type regularization of the TOV metric, (c.f. (2.9)), but rather we employ standard Schwarzschild coordinates, avoiding the singularity at A=0A=0 by working either inside or outside the Black Hole separately.

Our proceedure for shock matching is as follows: We first identify the shock surface across which a k=0k=0 FRW metric matches a TOV metric inside the Black Hole, such that the matching is Lipschitz continuous across the interface, and such that we have a smooth matching of the spheres of symmetry, (c.f., [13], Lemma 9, equation (5.3)). The Lipschitz matching of the metrics is guaranteed by a non-characteristic condition that always holds outside the Black Hole, when A>0,A>0, c.f. (5.23) below. Given this matching, we then determine a conservation constraint that guarantees that the Rankine-Hugoniot jump conditions

[Tμ​ν]​nμ=0,\displaystyle[T^{\mu\nu}]n_{\mu}=0, (5.1)

hold across the shock. (Here, as usual, [⋅][\cdot] denotes the jump in a quantity across the shock interface, nμn_{\mu} are the covariant components of the normal vector 𝐧{\bf n} to the shock surface, and assuming spherical symmetry, we need only require (5.1) for ν=0,1.\nu=0,1.) We can then apply [13], Lemma 9, which states that for metrics matched Lipschitz continuously across the shock, with a smooth matching of the spheres of symmetry, the Rankine-Hugoniot jump conditions (5.1) imply that the following equivalencies are also valid at the shock:

(i) The extrinsic curvature is continuous across the shock,

(ii) The Riemann and Einstein curvature tensors, viewed as second order operators on the metric components, produce no delta function sources on the shock,

(iii) In a neighborhood of each point on the shock surface there exist coordinate transformations such that in the new coordinates, all second derivatives of the metric components are bounded a.e., and

(iv) At each point on the shock surface there exist coordinate frames that are locally Lorentzian.

In the papers [13, 14, 17, 21], the main idea for carrying out this procedure in the case A>0,A>0, was to show that the single condition

[Tμ​ν]​nμ​nν=0,\displaystyle[T^{\mu\nu}]n_{\mu}n_{\nu}=0, (5.2)

alone implies the jump conditions (5.1), and hence (i)-(iv). However, we must modify this idea in the case A<0A<0 because it turns out that the condition (5.2) has a non-physical solution which everywhere violates the non-characteristic condition used to guarantee the Lipschitz matching of the metrics at the shock. For this reason, to obtain the conservation condition when the shock wave lies inside the Black Hole, we verify the Rankine-Hugoniot conditions directly.

To start, we match the FRW to the TOV metric when k=0k=0 and A<0.A<0. The k=0k=0 FRW metric in the usual (t,r)(t,r) coordinates is given by,

d​s2=−d​t2+R​(t)2​{d​r2+r2​d​Ω2}.ds^{2}=-dt^{2}+R(t)^{2}\left\{dr^{2}+r^{2}d\Omega^{2}\right\}. (5.3)

In (2.18)-(2.20) we showed that the mapping (t,r)→(r¯,t¯)(t,r)\rightarrow(\bar{r},\bar{t}) that takes metric (5.3) to standard Schwarzschild coordinates in which the metric takes the form,

d​s2=−BF​R​W​d​t¯2+AF​R​W−1​d​r¯2+r¯2​d​Ω2,ds^{2}=-B_{FRW}d\bar{t}^{2}+A_{FRW}^{-1}d\bar{r}^{2}+\bar{r}^{2}d\Omega^{2}, (5.4)

is given by

r¯\displaystyle\bar{r} =\displaystyle= R⁡(t)​r,\displaystyle R(t)r, (5.5)

and

d​t¯=(ψ​C)​d​t−(ψ​E)​d​r¯,\displaystyle d\bar{t}=(\psi C)dt-(\psi E)d\bar{r}, (5.6)

where

C\displaystyle C =\displaystyle= 1−H2​r¯2,\displaystyle 1-H^{2}\bar{r}^{2}, (5.7)
E\displaystyle E =\displaystyle= −r¯​H.\displaystyle-\bar{r}H. (5.8)

(Recall that ∂∂r¯\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{r}} is timelike in the coordinate system (r¯,t¯)(\bar{r},\bar{t}) and spacelike in the coordinate system (t,r¯)(t,\bar{r}) when AF​R​W<0,A_{FRW}<0, H−1>1.H^{-1}>1.) Here ψ\psi can be taken to be any solution of

∂∂r¯​(ψ​C)+∂∂t​(ψ​E)=0,\frac{\partial}{\partial\bar{r}}(\psi C)+\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\psi E)=0, (5.9)

determined from initial data on any non-characteristic surface, (c.f. the paragraph following (2.21)). Under this coordinate transformation, we obtain

AF​R​W−1\displaystyle A_{FRW}^{-1} =\displaystyle= R2R2−r¯2​R˙2=11−(r¯​H)2,\displaystyle\frac{R^{2}}{R^{2}-\bar{r}^{2}\dot{R}^{2}}=\frac{1}{1-\left(\bar{r}H\right)^{2}}, (5.10)
BF​R​W\displaystyle B_{FRW} =\displaystyle= 1ψ2​R2R2−r¯2​R˙2=1ψ2​11−(r¯​H)2,\displaystyle\frac{1}{\psi^{2}}\frac{R^{2}}{R^{2}-\bar{r}^{2}\dot{R}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\psi^{2}}\frac{1}{1-\left(\bar{r}H\right)^{2}}, (5.11)

c.f. (2.18)-(2.20). We use the subscript F​R​WFRW to distinguish the FRW metric coefficients AF​R​W=1−2​MF​R​Wr¯A_{FRW}=1-\frac{2M_{FRW}}{\bar{r}} and BF​R​WB_{FRW} from the TOV metric coefficients A=1−2​Mr¯A=1-\frac{2M}{\bar{r}} and B,B, that appear in the TOV line element

d​s2=−B​d​t¯2+A−1​d​r¯2+r¯2​d​Ω2,ds^{2}=-Bd\bar{t}^{2}+A^{-1}d\bar{r}^{2}+\bar{r}^{2}d\Omega^{2}, (5.12)

in standard Schwarzschild coordinates. By shock matching, using (2.7) and (5.10), we find that

MF​R​W​(t,r¯)=12​r¯3​H2=κ6​ρ​(t)​r¯3.M_{FRW}(t,\bar{r})=\frac{1}{2}\bar{r}^{3}H^{2}=\frac{\kappa}{6}\rho(t)\bar{r}^{3}. (5.13)

Assume now that the (r¯,t¯)(\bar{r},\bar{t}) coordinates that describe the TOV and FRW metrics in standard Schwarzschild coordinates, actually represent a single coordinate system for the pair of metrics matched across a shock surface where the metrics agree; that is, where A=AF​R​WA=A_{FRW} and B=BF​R​W.B=B_{FRW}. Setting AF​R​W=AA_{FRW}=A and using (5.13) gives

2​MF​R​Wr¯=(H​r¯)2=κ3​ρ​r¯2=2​Mr¯,\displaystyle\frac{2M_{FRW}}{\bar{r}}=(H\bar{r})^{2}=\frac{\kappa}{3}\rho\bar{r}^{2}=\frac{2M}{\bar{r}}, (5.14)

from which we deduce the following conservation of mass condition that must hold at the shock surface, and which is independent of ψ:\psi:

κ6​ρ​(t)​r¯3=M⁡(r¯).\displaystyle\frac{\kappa}{6}\rho(t)\bar{r}^{3}=M(\bar{r}). (5.15)

Equation (5.15) implicitly defines the shock surface r¯=r¯​(t),\bar{r}=\bar{r}(t), which then determines the position r=r⁡(t)=r¯​(t)R⁡(t)r=r(t)=\frac{\bar{r}(t)}{R(t)} of the shock in the original FRW coordinates (t,r).(t,r). By (5.14) we also see that

N≡1−A=2​Mr¯=(r¯​H)2,\displaystyle N\equiv 1-A=\frac{2M}{\bar{r}}=(\bar{r}H)^{2}, (5.16)

and so

r¯=N​H−1\displaystyle\bar{r}=\sqrt{N}H^{-1} (5.17)

holds on the shock surface. Using (5.17), we can interpret NN from the TOV metric as follows: if (t,r¯)(t,\bar{r}) is a point on the shock surface, then N⁡(t,r¯)\sqrt{N(t,\bar{r})} is equal to the number of Hubble lengths from the center of the FRW spacetime to the shock surface as measured at fixed time tt on the FRW side of the shock. Since N>1N>1 if and only if A<0,A<0, it follows that the shock wave lies beyond one Hubble length from the FRW center when A<0.A<0. Note that NN is a convenient variable because it appears in system (4.16)-(4.18).

Setting BF​R​W=BB_{FRW}=B at the shock surface and using (5.11), we obtain the initial condition for the integrating factor ψ\psi of the FRW metric on the shock surface (5.15); namely,

ψ=−+{(1−H2r¯2)B(r¯)}−1/2=−+{AB}−1/2,\displaystyle\psi=^{+}_{-}\left\{(1-H^{2}\bar{r}^{2})B(\bar{r})\right\}^{-1/2}=^{+}_{-}\left\{AB\right\}^{-1/2}, (5.18)

where we have used that 1−H2​r¯2=A<01-H^{2}\bar{r}^{2}=A<0 at the shock. Note that A​B>0,AB>0, and the choice of sign in (5.18) determines the time orientation for t¯,\bar{t}, c.f. (5.6).

We now derive a condition that guarantees that the surface r¯=r¯​(t)\bar{r}=\bar{r}(t) is non-characteristic when A<0.A<0.1010 10 This is no moot point. Indeed, in previous work, (c.f. [13, 14]), the authors used (5.2) to obtain the conservation constraint across the shock surface when A>0,A>0, but we must be careful here because a calculation shows that one of the solutions of (5.2) is everywhere characteristic for (5.9) when A<0.A<0. It follows that (5.1) does not hold across the characteristic surface, and so there is a solution of (5.2) that does not represent an actual weak solution of G=κ​TG=\kappa T when A<0.A<0. It is for this reason that we go directly to (5.1) to construct the conservation constraint in the case A<0A<0 below. To this end, differentiate (5.15) with respect to FRW time tt to obtain,

M′​r¯˙=κ6​ρ˙​r¯3+κ2​ρ​r¯2​r¯˙.\displaystyle M^{\prime}\dot{\bar{r}}=\frac{\kappa}{6}\dot{\rho}\bar{r}^{3}+\frac{\kappa}{2}\rho\bar{r}^{2}\dot{\bar{r}}. (5.19)

Using (2.8) and (4.17) in (5.19) we obtain the following formula for the speed r¯˙,\dot{\bar{r}}, the speed at which the shock wave is receding from an observer fixed at the FRW origin:

r¯˙=ρ+pρ+p¯​H​r¯.\displaystyle\dot{\bar{r}}=\frac{\rho+p}{\rho+\bar{p}}H\bar{r}. (5.20)

For future reference we record that this directly implies

r˙\displaystyle\dot{r} =\displaystyle= H​r¯R​(p−p¯ρ+p¯).\displaystyle\frac{H\bar{r}}{R}\left(\frac{p-\bar{p}}{\rho+\bar{p}}\right). (5.21)

On the other hand, in light of (2.21), the characteristics for (5.9) satisfy

r¯˙=−{r¯​H}−1+r¯​H.\displaystyle\dot{\bar{r}}=-\left\{\bar{r}H\right\}^{-1}+\bar{r}H. (5.22)

Thus the shock surface is characteristic if and only if the two speeds in (5.20) and (5.22) are equal, which holds if and only if

1−{ρ+pρ+p¯}=1(H​r¯)2.\displaystyle 1-\left\{\frac{\rho+p}{\rho+\bar{p}}\right\}=\frac{1}{(H\bar{r})^{2}}. (5.23)

Using (5.14) in (5.23) we conclude that the shock surface is non-characteristic for the PDE (5.9) if and only if

A≠ρ+pp−p¯.\displaystyle A\neq\frac{\rho+p}{p-\bar{p}}. (5.24)

The inequality (5.24) is not in general ruled out on a timelike shock surface when A<0.A<0. However, (5.24) immediately implies the following lemma which we record for use in Section 6:

Lemma 1

If ρ,p,ρ¯,p¯\rho,p,\bar{\rho},\bar{p} are all positive on the shock surface r¯=r¯​(t)\bar{r}=\bar{r}(t) defined implicitly by (5.15), then the surface is non-characteristic for the PDE (5.9) so long as p>p¯p>\bar{p} and A<0.A<0.

Assuming that (5.24) holds, the above procedure defines a mapping (t,r)→(r¯,t¯),(t,r)\rightarrow(\bar{r},\bar{t}), defined in a neighborhood of any point on the shock surface (r¯​(t),t),(\bar{r}(t),t), such that, under this coordinate identification, the FRW metric matches the TOV metric Lipshitz continuously across the shock surface. Note also that as in the OS solution, the coordinate r¯\bar{r} is timelike in the Schwarzschild coordinates (r¯,t¯)(\bar{r},\bar{t}) when A<0,A<0, but spacelike in the FRW coordinates (t,r¯),(t,\bar{r}), where the coordinate r¯\bar{r} measures arclength distance in each spatial slice t=c​o​n​s​t.t=const.

It remains to analyze the Rankine-Hugoniot jump conditions (5.1). The following theorem gives a formulation of the conservation constraint that is amenable to analysis.

Theorem 3

Assume that the coordinate mapping (t,r)→(r¯,t¯)(t,r)\rightarrow(\bar{r},\bar{t}) defines a Lipshitz continuous matching of an FRW metric to a TOV metric inside the Black Hole, in a neighborhood of a point PP across a non-characteristic shock surface r¯=r¯​(t)\bar{r}=\bar{r}(t) defined by (5.15), so that that N>1N>1 at P.P. Assume further that p,ρ>0p,\rho>0 at P.P. Then the Rankine-Hugoniot jump relations (5.1) together with the equivalent conditions (i)-(iv) listed after (5.1)) all hold at PP, if and only if the following single conservation constraint holds at the point P:P:

p¯=p−(ρ¯+pρ−ρ¯)​1N​ρ1+(ρ¯+pρ−ρ¯)​1N.\displaystyle\bar{p}=\frac{p-\left(\frac{\bar{\rho}+p}{\rho-\bar{\rho}}\right)\frac{1}{N}\rho}{1+\left(\frac{\bar{\rho}+p}{\rho-\bar{\rho}}\right)\frac{1}{N}}. (5.25)

Note that (5.25) immediately implies that if ρ>ρ¯,\rho>\bar{\rho}, then also p>p¯,p>\bar{p}, consistent with an outgoing explosion of an inner FRW metric into an outer TOV metric. (The construction of an explicit example of such a shock wave is the topic of the next section.) Solving for ρ¯\bar{\rho}, it follows that condition (5.25) is equivalent to the condition

ρ¯=−(ρ+p¯)​p+(p−p¯)​N​ρ(ρ+p¯)+(p−p¯)​N.\displaystyle\bar{\rho}=\frac{-\left(\rho+\bar{p}\right)p+(p-\bar{p})N\rho}{(\rho+\bar{p})+(p-\bar{p})N}. (5.26)

Note also that from (5.26) we see that if p=p¯=0,p=\bar{p}=0, then also ρ¯=0,\bar{\rho}=0, the conditions of the OS solution.

Before giving the proof of Theorem 3, we first use the conservation constraint (5.26) to derive the equations that describe the time evolution of the shock surface and TOV metric inside the Black Hole that matches a given k=0k=0 FRW metric at a shock wave positioned beyond one Hubble length N>1.N>1. To start, assume that ρ⁡(t),p⁡(t)\rho(t),p(t) and R⁡(t)R(t) are known functions of the FRW time tt that determine a unique equation of state p⁡(ρ),p(\rho), and let σ⁡(t)=p⁡(t)/ρ⁡(t).\sigma(t)=p(t)/\rho(t). The matching condition (5.15) written in the form

ρ=3​Nκ​r¯2,\displaystyle\rho=\frac{3N}{\kappa\bar{r}^{2}}, (5.27)

gives ρ\rho as a function of NN and r¯\bar{r} at the shock, and substituting this into the conservation constraint (5.26) and using p=p⁡(ρ)p=p(\rho) gives ρ¯\bar{\rho} as a function of p¯,N\bar{p},N and r¯.\bar{r}. The first two equations (4.16), (4.17) of the TOV system (4.16)-(4.18) then close upon substituting the resulting expression ρ¯=ρ¯​(p¯,N,r¯)\bar{\rho}=\bar{\rho}(\bar{p},N,\bar{r}) for ρ¯\bar{\rho} in the first equation (4.16). The resulting system,

p¯′\displaystyle\bar{p}^{\prime} =\displaystyle= p¯+ρ¯​(p¯,N,r¯)2​N′N−1,\displaystyle\frac{\bar{p}+\bar{\rho}(\bar{p},N,\bar{r})}{2}\frac{N^{\prime}}{N-1}, (5.28)
N′\displaystyle N^{\prime} =\displaystyle= −{Nr¯+κ​p¯​r¯},\displaystyle-\left\{\frac{N}{\bar{r}}+\kappa\bar{p}\bar{r}\right\}, (5.29)

then forms a non-autonomous system of two equations in the unknowns (p¯,N)(\bar{p},N) as a function of the independent variable r¯,\bar{r}, the shock position. (Again, “prime” denotes dd​r¯.\frac{d}{d\bar{r}}.) Solving (5.28), (5.29) gives p¯​(r¯)\bar{p}(\bar{r}) and N⁡(r¯)N(\bar{r}) subject to the initial conditions

p¯=p¯0,N=N0,a​t​r¯=r¯0.\displaystyle\bar{p}=\bar{p}_{0},\ N=N_{0},\ \ at\ \ \bar{r}=\bar{r}_{0}. (5.30)

Assuming the FRW solution ρ⁡(t),\rho(t), p⁡(t),p(t), and R⁡(t)R(t) is given, we can obtain r¯\bar{r} as a function of tt from (5.27), whereby we conclude that p¯​(r¯)\bar{p}(\bar{r}) and N⁡(r¯)N(\bar{r}) determine the entire shock wave solution. For example, to set the position of the shock at present time in the FRW metric to be at r¯=r¯0,\bar{r}=\bar{r}_{0}, choose ρ0=p​r​e​s​e​n​t​d​e​n​s​i​t​y,\rho_{0}=present\ density, define

N0=κ3​ρ0​r¯02,\displaystyle N_{0}=\frac{\kappa}{3}\rho_{0}\bar{r}_{0}^{2}, (5.31)

(c.f. use (5.27)). This leaves p¯0\bar{p}_{0} as a free parameter. Once we know the solution (p¯​(r¯),N​(r¯)),(\bar{p}(\bar{r}),N(\bar{r})), we can use (5.27) to obtain the FRW density ρ\rho as a function of r¯,\bar{r}, and inverting the relation

ρ⁡(t)=3​N​(r¯)κ​r¯2,\displaystyle\rho(t)=\frac{3N(\bar{r})}{\kappa\bar{r}^{2}}, (5.32)

gives the shock position r¯=r¯​(t),\bar{r}=\bar{r}(t), the distance from the shock wave to the FRW center at FRW time t.t. The FRW shock position is then

r⁡(t)=r¯​(t)R⁡(t).\displaystyle r(t)=\frac{\bar{r}(t)}{R(t)}.

The only other unknown in the problem is the metric coefficient B⁡(r¯)B(\bar{r}) from the TOV metric, which we get by integrating the equation (4.18)1111 11 Note that (5.33) completes the definition of the TOV metric, and so the integrating factor ψ\psi for the shock matching is determined by (5.18), and from this the non-characteristic condition (5.24) implies the Lipschitz matching of the metrics.,

B(r¯)=B0exp{−∫r0r1N⁡(ξ)−1(N⁡(ξ)ξ+κρ¯(ξ))dξ}.\displaystyle B(\bar{r})=B_{0}\exp{\left\{-\int_{r_{0}}^{r}\frac{1}{N(\xi)-1}\left(\frac{N(\xi)}{\xi}+\kappa\bar{\rho}(\xi)\right)d\xi\right\}}. (5.33)

Note that for an outgoing shock wave in an expanding FRW metric, it follows from (5.29) that NN decreases and r¯\bar{r} increases in forward FRW time, and so N→∞,N\rightarrow\infty, r¯→0\bar{r}\rightarrow 0 would correspond to the Big Bang from the FRW point of view.

We conclude that the problem of constructing FRW-TOV shock waves with N>1N>1 reduces to the analysis of the 2×22\times 2 system (5.28), (5.29). The next theorem shows that when we make the change of variable p¯→u=p¯ρ\bar{p}\rightarrow u=\frac{\bar{p}}{\rho} and take NN to be the independent variable, the resulting equivalent system has the nice property that the equations are coupled to the FRW metric only through the variable σ=pρ.\sigma=\frac{p}{\rho}.

Theorem 4

Under the change of variables

u=p¯ρ,v=ρ¯ρ,σ=pρ,\displaystyle u=\frac{\bar{p}}{\rho},\ v=\frac{\bar{\rho}}{\rho},\ \sigma=\frac{p}{\rho}, (5.34)

system (5.28), (5.29) with conservation constraint (5.26) transforms to the equivalent system

d​ud​N=−{(1+u)2​(1+3​u)​N}​{(3​u−1)​(σ−u)​N+6​u​(1+u)(σ−u)​N+(1+u)},\displaystyle\frac{du}{dN}=-\left\{\frac{(1+u)}{2(1+3u)N}\right\}\left\{\frac{(3u-1)(\sigma-u)N+6u(1+u)}{(\sigma-u)N+(1+u)}\right\}, (5.35)
d​r¯d​N\displaystyle\frac{d\bar{r}}{dN} =\displaystyle= −11+3​u​r¯N,\displaystyle-\frac{1}{1+3u}\frac{\bar{r}}{N}, (5.36)

with conservation constraint

v=−σ⁡(1+u)+(σ−u)​N(1+u)+(σ−u)​N.\displaystyle v=\frac{-\sigma\left(1+u\right)+(\sigma-u)N}{(1+u)+(\sigma-u)N}. (5.37)

For such solutions, the speed of the shock interface relative to the fluid comoving on the FRW side of the shock, is given by

s=R​r˙=N​(σ−u1+u).\displaystyle s=R\dot{r}=\sqrt{N}\left(\frac{\sigma-u}{1+u}\right). (5.38)

Note that the dependence of (5.35)-(5.37) on the FRW metric is only through the variable σ,\sigma, and hence (5.35) is coupled to (5.36) only through the function σ.\sigma. In particular, if we assume that σ\sigma is constant in the FRW metric, (a reasonable model problem, c.f. [14]), then equation (5.35) uncouples from equation (5.36) to form a non-autonomous scalar equation in uu and NN which is amenable to phase plane analysis. This is the starting point for the exact solutions constructed in the next section.

Note too that since (5.36) implies that d​Nd​r¯<0,\frac{dN}{d\bar{r}}<0, and N\sqrt{N} gives the number of Hubble lengths to the shock wave, c.f. (5.17), equation (5.36) implies that the number of Hubble lengths from the FRW center to the shock wave decreases in time, as claimed in the introduction.

Since system system (5.35), (5.36) is equivalent to system (5.28), (5.29), the former system also determines all quantities in the shock wave solution, but now as a function of the variable N.N. For example, a solution of system (5.35), (5.36) is determined by the initial conditions u=u0u=u_{0} and r¯=r¯0\bar{r}=\bar{r}_{0} at N=N0,N=N_{0}, which entails assigning three constants. Alternatively, if we ask that the shock wave be positioned N0\sqrt{N_{0}} Hubble lengths from the FRW center at the present FRW value of the density ρ=ρ0,\rho=\rho_{0}, then by (5.27), the initial shock position is determined by

r¯0=3​N0κ​ρ0,\displaystyle\bar{r}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{3N_{0}}{\kappa\rho_{0}}}, (5.39)

and there is then a one parameter family of such solutions (u​(N),r¯​(N))(u(N),\bar{r}(N)) determined by the remaining free parameter

u0=p¯0ρ0.\displaystyle u_{0}=\frac{\bar{p}_{0}}{\rho_{0}}. (5.40)

Once we know the solution (u​(N),r¯​(N)),(u(N),\bar{r}(N)), we can use

ρ=3​Nκ​[r¯​(N)]2,\displaystyle\rho=\frac{3N}{\kappa\left[\bar{r}(N)\right]^{2}}, (5.41)

to obtain ρ⁡(N),\rho(N), the FRW density ρ\rho as a function of NN at the shock. Since the FRW metric is known, knowing ρ⁡(N)\rho(N) determines p⁡(N)p(N) and σ⁡(N)=p⁡(N)ρ⁡(N),\sigma(N)=\frac{p(N)}{\rho(N)}, and using these in (5.37) we obtain v⁡(N)v(N) and ρ¯​(N)=v​(N)​ρ​(N).\bar{\rho}(N)=v(N)\rho(N). Finally, the TOV metric coefficient BB is determined as a function of NN by integrating the equation (4.18) with respect to N,N, yielding the formula

B(r¯)=B0exp{−∫N0N1ξ−1(ξr¯​(ξ)+κρ¯(ξ))dξ}.\displaystyle B(\bar{r})=B_{0}\exp{\left\{-\int_{N_{0}}^{N}\frac{1}{\xi-1}\left(\frac{\xi}{\bar{r}(\xi)}+\kappa\bar{\rho}(\xi)\right)d\xi\right\}}. (5.42)

To connect NN with the FRW time t,t, invert the relation (5.41), obtaining N⁡(t).N(t). Since R⁡(t)R(t) is assumed known, we can use

r⁡(t)=r¯​(N​(t))R⁡(t),\displaystyle r(t)=\frac{\bar{r}(N(t))}{R(t)}, (5.43)

to get the FRW shock position rr as a function of t.t. Relations (5.39)-(5.43) formally determine an exact shock wave solution of the Einstein equations for any given (k=0)(k=0) FRW metric, and any given solution of system (5.35), (5.36).

We summarize the results in this section as follows: System (5.35)-(5.36) describes the TOV metrics that match a given k=0k=0 FRW metric across a shock wave discontinuity when A<0,A<0, assuming that the conservation constraint (5.37) is satisfied. Solutions of these equations, together with the initial conditions in (5.39)-(5.43), determine weak solutions of the Einstein equations containing a shock wave interface across which the metric is only Lipschitz continuous, and such that conditions (i)-(iv) (after (5.2)) are satisfied. Since the resulting solutions are formally time-reversible, it still remains to impose a physically meaningful entropy condition. The entropy condition for shocks determines the time orientation of the solution, c.f. [12]. In the next section we construct a class of exact solutions of these equations which satisfy an entropy condition that agrees with the entropy condition of gas dynamics in the non-relativistic limit.

6 Exact Shock Wave Solutions When A<0.A<0.

In this section we derive a class of exact solutions of equations (5.35)-(5.36) in the case when the FRW pressure is given by the equation of state

p=σ​ρ,\displaystyle p=\sigma\rho, (6.1)

where σ\sigma is assumed to be constant,

0<σ<1.\displaystyle 0<\sigma<1. (6.2)

In this section, as an entropy condition, we impose the condition that the shock be compressive, a condition sufficient to choose the physically relevant stable shocks in classical gas dynamics, [4, 7, 12]. That is, we will require that the pressure and density be larger on the side of the shock that receives the mass flux. Exact solutions satisfying the equation of state (6.1) were constructed in [14] for the case A>0,A>0, so we can interpret the results here as an extension of the results in [14] to the case A<0.A<0. However, in [14], the conservation constraint led to a TOV equation of state also of the form (6.1), but in our case here, the TOV pressure is not so simple due to the fact that the conservation constraint (5.37) is of a different form.

Assuming (6.1), the solution to the FRW equations (2.7), (2.8) is given in Theorem 2, equations (2.37)-(2.41), and we assume an expanding universe, (R˙>0\dot{R}>0), with initial conditions R=0R=0 at t=0,t=0, and R=1,R=1, at t=t0.t=t_{0}. The solution has one assignable constant which can be taken to be t0,t_{0}, ρ0\rho_{0} or H0,H_{0}, since

ρ0\displaystyle\rho_{0} =\displaystyle= 43​κ​(1+σ)2​1t02,\displaystyle\frac{4}{3\kappa(1+\sigma)^{2}}\frac{1}{t_{0}^{2}}, (6.3)
H0=[3​(1+σ)2]​1t0,\displaystyle H_{0}=\left[\frac{3(1+\sigma)}{2}\right]\frac{1}{t_{0}}, (6.4)

where we interpret t0t_{0} as ‘‘present time’’in the FRW metric1313 13 Since we are assuming the idealized equation of state (6.1) for the FRW metric, the value of the Hubble constant at present time alone determines the solution. In the standard model of cosmology based on a k=0k=0 FRW metric, [1], the solution is determined by two assignable constants, the Hubble constant H0H_{0} and the background radiation temperature T0,T_{0}, [1, 21]. Assuming (6.1), the freedom to assign T0T_{0} is represented by the freedom to assign σ.\sigma. Also, in the standard model the galaxies follow the particle paths of the matter field after the time when the pressure of the matter field is essentially zero. In the model (6.1), the matter is co-moving with respect to the radial coordinate r,r, and hence the particle paths follow r˙=0.\dot{r}=0. Loosely speaking, we refer to the motion along the particle paths as the motion of the galaxies in the cosmological interpretation of a general FRW metric. Thus we say that the shock wave is exploding outward through the galaxies when the shock wave satisfies r˙>0,\dot{r}>0,, and the relations (5.39)-(5.43) hold.

We now solve the TOV shock equations (5.35)-(5.36), to obtain a shock wave solution that matches this FRW metric for all R⁡(t)R(t) in the interval between R=0R=0 and R=1.R=1. Since (5.35) is coupled to (5.36) only through the function σ,\sigma, our assumption that σ\sigma is constant in the FRW metric implies that solutions of system (5.35)-(5.36) are determined by solutions of the scalar non-autonomous equation (5.35). Making the change of variable S=1/N,S=1/N, (we do this to transform the “Big Bang” N→∞N\rightarrow\infty over to rest point at S→0,S\rightarrow 0, c.f. [21]), equation (5.35) takes the form

d​ud​S={(1+u)2​(1+3​u)​S}​{(3​u−1)​(σ−u)+6​u​(1+u)​S(σ−u)+(1+u)​S},\displaystyle\frac{du}{dS}=\left\{\frac{(1+u)}{2(1+3u)S}\right\}\left\{\frac{(3u-1)(\sigma-u)+6u(1+u)S}{(\sigma-u)+(1+u)S}\right\}, (6.5)

where u=p¯/ρ.u=\bar{p}/\rho. We now construct solutions of (6.5) that model the “Big Bang” as a localized explosion with an outgoing blast wave emanating from r¯=0\bar{r}=0 at time t=0.t=0. Thus, motivated by classical gas dynamics, we seek solutions of (6.5) that satisfy the entropy conditions,

0<p¯<p,\displaystyle 0<\bar{p}<p, (6.6)
0<ρ¯<ρ,\displaystyle 0<\bar{\rho}<\rho, (6.7)

and meet the physical bounds on the TOV equation of state

0<p¯<ρ¯.\displaystyle 0<\bar{p}<\bar{\rho}. (6.8)

Conditions (6.6), (6.7) for outgoing shock waves imply that the shock wave is compressive. The condition (6.8) implies that the TOV equation of state is physically reasonable. Note that the conditions N>1N>1 and 0<p¯<p0<\bar{p}<p restrict the domain of (6.5) to the region 0<u<σ<1,0<u<\sigma<1, 0<S<1.0<S<1. 6.4 The asymptotics for S≥1S\geq 1

Equation (6.18) implies that v≡ρ¯ρ=0=ρ¯v\equiv\frac{\bar{\rho}}{\rho}=0=\bar{\rho} at S=1.S=1. Thus, the TOV metric inside the Black Hole continues to the empty space Schwarzschild metric at u=0,u=0, v=0,v=0, S=1,S=1, an event horizon for the outer TOV metric in light of the fact that at S=1,S=1, N=2​Mr¯=1,N=\frac{2M}{\bar{r}}=1, c.f. (5.17). It follows that if the FRW density ρ\rho is small at S=1,S=1, then it makes sense in cosmology to approximate the FRW solution with p=0p=0 for all times S≥1.S\geq 1. Assuming this, Theorem 6 implies that for each 0<σ<1,0<\sigma<1, the unique solution uσ​(S)u_{\sigma}(S) continues to the zero pressure, k=0,k=0, OS solution at S=N=1,S=N=1, the moment when the shock wave lies exactly one Hubble length from the FRW center. That is, at S=1,S=1, the shock wave emerges from the White Hole event horizon of an ambient Schwarzschild metric as an outward propagating contact discontinuity that bounds a finite FRW mass, this being exactly equal to the total mass of the ambiant Schwarzschild metric into which it propagates. Thereafter the interface continues out to infinity along a geodesic of the Schwarzschild metric outside the Black Hole.

We conclude that the OS solution gives the large time asymptotics of this new class of shock wave solutions that evolve inside of a Black Hole—and thus the explosion that begins at the Big Bang eventually settles down to a localized expansion that looks something like a giant supernovae, but on an enormous scale. .
